title: Distributed tracing
problem: A checkout takes two seconds across nine services and nobody can say which hop or query spent the time, because each service sees only its own slice.
summary: A trace is the tree of spans one request creates across services, joined by a trace id carried in the W3C traceparent header. OpenTelemetry produces it, sampling keeps it affordable, and the waterfall view shows where the time went.
catTip: Every room my mouse runs through gets the same tracking number scratched on the floor. Afterwards I read the trail like a map: which room cost the most time, and where it went round in forty tiny circles.

recall.q: How does a span in the payment service end up in the same trace as the gateway's span?
recall.a: The gateway sends a traceparent header carrying the trace id, its own span id and a sampled flag. The payment service reads it, creates a child span with that span id as parent and the same trace id, and forwards a new traceparent downstream; the backend stitches the spans together by trace id.

guide.breaks: Without propagated context each service records its timings in isolation, so a slow request becomes a nine-way argument, N+1 query storms hide in plain sight, and the one failing request in a thousand leaves no connected record.
guide.tradeoffs: Recording every span of every request is unaffordable, so you sample and lose detail; tail sampling needs stateful collectors; and context must cross every hop, including message queues, or the trace breaks in two.
guide.explainSimply: A trace follows one request like a parcel with a tracking number scanned at every depot. Each service adds its own step with a start and end time, and the tracking number travels in a header so the steps can be stitched together. The result reads like a timeline that shows exactly where the waiting happened.
guide.hint: Think about what has to travel with the request so that two services can agree they worked on the same one.

meow: One tracking number, many depots, one timeline. The slow depot cannot hide from the waterfall.

quiz.prompt: A request arrives with the header traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01. What does the final 01 mean?
options: The trace contains one span so far
The caller is recording this trace, so this service should record its spans too
This is version 1 of the Trace Context specification
The request is a retry of an earlier attempt
quiz.explanation: The last field is trace-flags, and its lowest bit is the sampled flag; the version is the first field, 00. Nothing in the header counts spans or marks retries.

quiz.prompt: You want to keep every trace that contains an error while recording only 1% of normal traffic. Which approach does this require?
options: Head-based sampling at 1%, since errors will be represented in proportion
Tail-based sampling in a collector that sees all the spans of a trace before deciding
Head-based sampling at 100% in the services that produce most errors
Logging the errors instead, since traces cannot capture failures
quiz.explanation: Whether a trace contains an error is only known once its spans have completed, so the decision must be made at the tail by a collector holding the whole trace. Head-based sampling at 1% is the strongest distractor: it keeps 1% of error traces too, which means losing 99 of every 100 failures you wanted to see.

cards.q: In a waterfall you see 40 identical 10 ms database spans in a staircase under one handler span. Name the pattern and the fix.
cards.a: The N+1 pattern: one query per item in a loop. Batch the lookups into a single query or bulk call (or fetch them in parallel), and the staircase collapses into one short span.

cards.q: Why does tail-based sampling need all spans of a trace to reach the same collector instance, and how is that arranged at scale?
cards.a: The decision depends on the whole trace (an error in any span, total latency), and spans arrive from many services. A first tier of collectors routes spans by trace id to a second tier that buffers each trace for a decision window (30 seconds by default in the OpenTelemetry Collector) and then keeps or drops it whole.

glossary.note: The CNCF project, formed by merging OpenTracing and OpenCensus, that defines vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs and a Collector for traces, metrics and logs.

sources.title: W3C Recommendation, "Trace Context" (23 November 2021)
sources.supports: traceparent format version-trace-id-parent-id-trace-flags; field sizes 1, 16, 8 and 1 bytes; version 00; sampled flag as the least significant bit; all-zero ids invalid; the example header value; tracestate for vendor-specific pairs

sources.title: OpenTelemetry docs, "Traces" (concepts)
sources.supports: span fields (name, parent span id, timestamps, context, attributes, events, links, status); span kinds Client, Server, Internal, Producer, Consumer; the root span has no parent; context propagation as the enabling concept

sources.title: OpenTelemetry docs, "Sampling" (concepts)
sources.supports: head sampling decides as early as possible and cannot use whole-trace data; tail sampling considers all or most spans, can keep every error, and requires stateful components; Collector sampling processors

sources.title: OpenTelemetry specification, "Tracing SDK" (Sampling)
sources.supports: the default sampler is ParentBased(root=AlwaysOn); ratio-based sampling must be deterministic on the trace id and is recommended for root spans with ParentBased

sources.title: OpenTelemetry Collector Contrib, "Tail Sampling Processor" README
sources.supports: decision_wait default 30 s; policies such as status_code and latency; all spans of a trace must reach the same collector instance; two collector layers with a load-balancing exporter

sources.title: OpenTelemetry docs, "What is OpenTelemetry?"
sources.supports: vendor- and tool-agnostic framework of APIs, SDKs and a Collector; a CNCF project formed by merging OpenTracing and OpenCensus; covers traces, metrics and logs; not an observability backend

sources.title: Sigelman et al., "Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure", Google, 2010
sources.supports: spans with a span id and parent id forming a trace tree; adequate trace data for high-volume services at a sampling rate as low as 1/1024 (read from the paper's PDF)
